issues.legal_issue: Secondary evidence of a document is inadmissible unless the failure to produce the original is accounted for and the copy is supported by foundational evidence establishing its authenticity.
material_facts: The party seeking specific performance relied on a photocopy of a power of attorney to establish that the property owner had authorised a representative to sell the property.
The original power of attorney was not produced, and no factual foundation was laid to justify reliance on secondary evidence.
The property owner admitted his signature on the photocopy but did not admit its contents or genuineness.
issues.conclusion: The trial court could not treat the photocopy as proof that the power of attorney authorised the representative to sell the property; secondary evidence could not be relied upon without the required foundation and proof.
issues.legal_principle: Section 65 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 permits secondary evidence only subject to its statutory conditions. When the original is not produced, its absence must be accounted for, and foundational evidence must establish that the copy is a true copy. The Court relied on The Roman Catholic Mission v. State of Madras, AIR 1966 SC 1457; State of Rajasthan v. Khemraj, AIR 2000 SC 1759; Life Insurance Corporation of India v. Ram Pal Singh Bisen, (2010) 4 SCC 491; and M. Chandra v. M. Thangamuthu, (2010) 9 SCC 712.

rule.if: civil_document_proof_case and secondary_evidence_tendered and original_not_produced and not nonproduction_accounted_for and not copy_authenticated

predicates.civil_document_proof_case: A party in a civil case relies on a document to establish a material fact.
predicates.secondary_evidence_tendered: A party offers a copy or other secondary evidence of the document instead of its original.
predicates.original_not_produced: The original document is not produced in court.
predicates.nonproduction_accounted_for: The party relying on secondary evidence establishes a legally recognised reason why the original is not produced.
predicates.copy_authenticated: Foundational evidence establishes that the offered copy is a true copy of the original.

issues.definition: When a party in a civil document-proof case offers a copy without producing the original, the copy is inadmissible if the absence of the original is not accounted for and the copy is not authenticated.

issues.legal_issue: Admission of a document, or of a signature appearing on it, does not by itself prove the document’s contents or establish the probative value of those contents.
material_facts: The property owner acknowledged his signature on the photocopy of the power of attorney but denied admitting its contents or genuineness.
The trial court inferred from the signature admission that the document authorised the representative to sell the property.
The Supreme Court held that the court had to assess the document’s probative value and could not draw that inference from the signature admission alone.
issues.conclusion: The signature admission did not establish the contents of the power of attorney or prove that it authorised a sale; the trial court’s contrary inference was unwarranted.
issues.legal_principle: Admissibility and probative value are distinct, and a document that is admitted in evidence does not thereby become proof of its contents. The Court relied on State of Bihar v. Sri Radha Krishna Singh, AIR 1983 SC 684, and Madan Mohan Singh v. Rajni Kant, AIR 2010 SC 2933.

predicates.civil_evidence_case: A court is deciding a civil dispute using documentary evidence.
predicates.document_admitted: A document or a copy of it has been admitted or received in evidence.
predicates.contents_not_admitted_or_proven: The relevant contents of the document have not themselves been admitted or established by evidence.

issues.definition: In a civil evidence case, admitting a document does not prove its contents when those contents have not themselves been admitted or established.

issues.legal_issue: A first appellate court must independently assess the material evidence and decide all relevant issues with reasons rather than merely express general agreement or address only selected issues.
material_facts: The High Court was deciding a first appeal from a decree for specific performance.

It formulated issues but did not decide whether the property owner had executed a power of attorney authorising the representative to alienate the property, despite that issue being central to the dispute.
The High Court did not independently assess and discuss the relevant evidence and issues before deciding the appeal.
issues.conclusion: The High Court failed to comply with the requirements governing first appeals because it did not independently assess the evidence and give reasoned findings on the relevant issues.
issues.legal_principle: Order XLI Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 requires a first appellate court to formulate the points for determination, decide them, and give reasons. The first appeal is a valuable right involving rehearing on fact and law. The Court relied on Thakur Sukhpal Singh v. Thakur Kalyan Singh, AIR 1963 SC 146; Girijanandini Devi v. Bijendra Narain Choudhary, AIR 1967 SC 1124; G. Amalorpavam v. R.C. Diocese of Madurai, (2006) 3 SCC 224; Shiv Kumar Sharma v. Santosh Kumari, (2007) 8 SCC 600; Gannmani Anasuya v. Parvatini Amarendra Chowdhary, AIR 2007 SC 2380; B.V. Nagesh v. H.V. Sreenivasa Murthy, JT (2010) 10 SCC 551; Santosh Hazari v. Purushottam Tiwari, (2001) 3 SCC 179; and Madhukar v. Sangram, (2001) 4 SCC 756.

predicates.first_appeal: The proceeding is a first appeal from a trial court’s decision.
predicates.material_issues_require_decision: The appeal raises material issues that must be resolved to decide the case.
predicates.appellate_court_does_not_independently_a: The appellate court fails to evaluate the relevant evidence independently and to decide the material issues with reasons.

issues.definition: In a first appeal involving material issues, failure to assess the relevant evidence independently requires reasoned findings on those issues.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate judgment cannot stand when the courts have not adjudicated the case in accordance with law, and the matter may be remitted for a fresh decision addressing the unresolved issues.
material_facts: The trial court treated a photocopy and an admission of a signature as establishing the contents and effect of a power of attorney without the required evidentiary foundation.
The High Court did not decide the central issue concerning the alleged authority to sell and did not independently assess the relevant evidence.
The Supreme Court did not decide the merits of the claims concerning adequacy of consideration or the rise in property prices.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s judgment and remitted the matter to it for a fresh decision in accordance with law, without expressing a view that would prejudice either side on the merits.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the requirements for proof of secondary evidence under Section 65 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 and the duties of a first appellate court under Order XLI Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. It concluded that the courts below had not adjudicated the case strictly in accordance with law and remitted it for reconsideration.

predicates.civil_first_appeal: The proceeding is a first appeal in a civil case.
predicates.trial_court_used_unproved_document_as_pr: The trial court relied on a document whose relevant contents or authenticity had not been established in accordance with law.
predicates.appellate_court_failed_to_decide_materia: The appellate court did not independently decide material issues necessary to resolve the case.

issues.definition: When a civil first appeal follows reliance on an unproved document and the appellate court leaves material issues undecided, the appellate judgment is set aside and the case is remitted.
